A call payoff and its profit are different

Predict: does finishing above the strike guarantee a profit after paying the premium?

Original hypothetical teaching example. This complete static route needs no JavaScript or animation. The interactive walkthrough is available inside the chapter.

On a narrow screen, scroll the diagram horizontally. Every value and step is also explained below.

Step 4/4: Terminal price £120
Strike £100; premium £5. Payoff=max(120−100,0)=£20. Profit=payoff−5=£15. The premium is paid even when the option expires without value.

All steps and numerical explanations

  1. Terminal price £80

    Strike £100; premium £5. Payoff=max(80−100,0)=£0. Profit=payoff−5=£-5. The premium is paid even when the option expires without value.

  2. Terminal price £100

    Strike £100; premium £5. Payoff=max(100−100,0)=£0. Profit=payoff−5=£-5. The premium is paid even when the option expires without value.

  3. Terminal price £105

    Strike £100; premium £5. Payoff=max(105−100,0)=£5. Profit=payoff−5=£0. Break-even occurs at £105, not £100.

  4. Terminal price £120

    Strike £100; premium £5. Payoff=max(120−100,0)=£20. Profit=payoff−5=£15. The premium is paid even when the option expires without value.

One hypothetical European call at expiry, one unit, no fees, interest, dividends or exercise complications. The premium here is assumed, not a model-derived fair value.
